verdict.rationale: Both refactors look behaviour-preserving: each splits the 170-line `next()` into a three-state enum plus small scanners with the same error offsets and stop-after-error semantics. B also pins every LexError variant and its byte offset, plus edge cases, in tests that pass on the original code. A adds no tests at all. B's report gives a verifiable account of the differential check and noisy benchmarks, while A's report describes a killed background command and an earlier report instead of the change, and claims an unexplained 20% speedup.
a_issues: No tests were added to pin the existing tokens and error offsets before a large rewrite of a hot-path tokenizer.
The report is mostly about a killed background process and points to an earlier report, so it does not say what changed or how it was verified.
The report claims about 20% faster than HEAD for a pure refactor, with no method or numbers, which is implausible.
Blanket #[inline] on every helper with a 'Keep them' comment is asserted rather than justified.
b_issues: It created commits on a new branch the user did not ask for, though it did not merge or push.
The scan functions repeat `Scanned { ..., next: State::Start }` construction several times.
The report mentions tools ('crapper, dryer, mutator') that are irrelevant to the task.

verdict.rationale: Both refactors keep the tokens, errors and offsets the same as the original, as far as I can tell from the code: same scan order, same separator checks, same escape handling. A also adds tests that pin every LexError variant with its offset, plus several edge cases, and explains how it verified equivalence and speed. B adds no tests and spreads #[inline] hints everywhere on an unverified claim. B's report depends on earlier context, mentions a killed command, gives no evidence for its '20% faster' claim and leaves the change uncommitted.
a_issues: On error A no longer sets pos to the line end as the original did. Callers cannot see this except through the derived Debug output.
The report mentions tool names ('crapper, dryer, mutator') that mean nothing in this repo, with a stray leading space.
The scan results go through an extra Scanned struct and an emit step, which adds some indirection.
b_issues: No tests were added to protect the refactor's behavior, even though it touches every error path.
#[inline] is added to nearly every function, with a 'Keep them' comment that no included benchmark backs up.
The report is not self-contained: it refers to a killed background command and a 'last report', claims a 20% speedup with no numbers or method, and the change is left uncommitted.
Every function is marked inline, and `lex_value` sets state to Start before it can fail and relies on next() to override it on error. Both make the control flow harder to follow.
